title: Reading a mishnah
hook: a case, a few opinions, and often an anonymous ruling

segments.voice: Yesterday, family purity: apart, then together, kept quietly by the couples who keep it. Your line was a private practice. Did you let someone's quiet observance be? Day one thousand ninety-one.

From what time may the Shema be recited in the evening? That's the question that opens the tractate Berakhot. Not why. Not whether. When. And the answer doesn't come in one voice. It comes as a small crowd: Rabbi Eliezer, then the Sages, then Rabban Gamliel. And then, as if the page can't help itself, a story about Rabban Gamliel's sons coming home late from a wedding. We've walked through the six orders of the Mishnah. Now we start on how the Talmud works, with how to read a single mishnah.
screen: `FROM WHAT TIME?` → `A SMALL CROWD OF VOICES.` → `SONS HOME LATE FROM A WEDDING.`

segments.voice: Reading a mishnah. Take it in four moves. First, the case. A mishnah tends to start with a concrete question, and this one answers with a picture, not a clock: from the hour the priests go in to eat their holy portion. Those are priests who were impure, who immersed, and who waited for evening. Water and time, from the last few days, become the start of the evening prayer. Second, the voices. Until when? Rabbi Eliezer says, until the end of the first watch of the night. The Sages say, until midnight. Rabban Gamliel says, until dawn rises. Three answers, each with a name, and the Mishnah keeps all three. Third, the story. Rabban Gamliel's sons come home from a wedding feast and tell him they haven't said the Shema. He tells them: if dawn hasn't risen, you are still obliged to say it. Then the Mishnah turns to the Sages' midnight and explains it: they set it as a fence, to keep people far from missing it. So the stricter voice turns out to be a guardrail, not a different law. Fourth, the voice with no name. Here, no one argues over the start; the debate is only about the end. In other mishnahs a ruling is given with no name at all. A line like that is called stam, plain. The Talmud has a saying that an unnamed mishnah is Rabbi Meir's, and readers learn to listen hard for that plain voice. Put the moves together and you have a way to read any mishnah. Find the case. Hear each voice by name. Watch for a story. Then listen for who speaks without a name.
screen: `THE CASE: FROM THE PRIESTS' MEAL.` · `THE VOICES: WATCH, MIDNIGHT, DAWN.` · `THE STORY, AND A FENCE.` · `STAM: THE VOICE WITH NO NAME.` · then, large: `A CASE, THEN VOICES.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: read one mishnah slowly. No book needed; take the one you just heard. Sit, and let your breath settle. Say the question to yourself: from what time, until what time? Then let each voice speak in turn, by name. Rabbi Eliezer. The Sages. Rabban Gamliel. Picture the sons at the door, late, a little worried. Which voice do you lean toward? Notice that the page never makes you choose. It keeps them all. The bell holds the time.
Reading a mishnah. A case, a few named voices, sometimes a story, and a plain voice with no name, all kept on one page. Today's word.
Your line: a case, then voices. Today, when a question comes up at home or at work, name every voice in the room before you pick one. Day one thousand ninety-one.

howItsDone: Jews who study Mishnah sometimes learn it with a partner or in a class, reading each mishnah aloud, naming its case and its voices, and some study a set amount each day.

fork.setup: you're Rabban Gamliel's son, home from a wedding feast after midnight, and you haven't said the evening Shema. you ask your father. what does he say?
options: too late. the Sages said midnight.
if dawn hasn't risen, you still have to say it.
skip it and say it twice tomorrow.
fork.reveal: he tells them: if dawn hasn't risen, you are obliged to say it. the Mishnah then explains the Sages' midnight as a fence.

original.note: Hebrew: a single teaching of the Mishnah, and the name of the whole collection.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rule book with one answer per question.
what it means: a case, a few named opinions, sometimes a story, and sometimes a plain voice with no name, all kept on the page.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 1:1: the priests at nightfall, Eliezer's first watch, the Sages' midnight as a fence, Rabban Gamliel's dawn, and his sons home from a wedding.
